title: Why do stars twinkle (and planets mostly don't)?
description: Twinkle, twinkle is not the star's fault. The wobble happens in the air above your head — and planets escape it for a simple reason.

body.heading: The star is steady; the air is not
paragraphs: A star's light travels through space in a straight, steady beam. The trouble starts in the last few kilometres, in Earth's atmosphere, where layers of warm and cool air are always sliding over each other.

Each layer bends light slightly differently, so the beam gets jiggled thousands of times a second. Your eye sees the star brighten, dim and seem to jump — the effect astronomers call scintillation, and everyone else calls twinkling.

body.heading: Why planets shine steadily
paragraphs: Stars are so far away that even through a telescope they are points of light, and a point is easy to push around. Planets are much closer, so they appear as tiny discs. The air jiggles each part of the disc differently, and the jiggles average out — so planets usually shine with a calm, steady light.
That gives you a field test on any clear night: a bright “star” that refuses to twinkle is very likely a planet. Venus and Jupiter are the usual suspects.

body.heading: Twinkle as a weather report
paragraphs: Astronomers watch twinkling closely, because strong twinkling means turbulent air and blurry telescope views — they call it bad “seeing”. The steadiest skies sit above high, dry mountains and calm oceans, which is exactly where the great observatories are built.
Next time the stars are dancing, remember: you are not watching the stars misbehave. You are watching the air itself, made visible.

takeaway: Stars twinkle because turbulent air bends their pinpoint light; planets look steady because their tiny discs average the wobble out.
